newsitem.title: GERMANY: No breakthrough, but German tax talks to continue.
newsitem.headline: No breakthrough, but German tax talks to continue.

text.p: Germany's ruling parties and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) made no early breakthrough on Monday in a rare summit on tax reforms aimed at fighting record post-war unemployment, but they plan to meet again this week.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel said a six-strong working group would meet on Friday. Wolfgang Gerhardt, leader of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), said he hoped a broad deal on tax reforms could be reached by Easter.

But the two sides ended their meeting still unhappy with each other's ideas of how to pay for tax cuts without throwing into doubt lasting compliance with the fiscal demands of European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"There was no narrowing of the gap between our two positions," SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine told a news conference after the three-hour talks.

Government sources reacted cautiously to the meeting. "We must simply see how further talks go," one said. SPD officials, meanwhile, said they saw a chance to agree cuts in high German labour overheads. "Here, there is movement. Not enough, but still," one SPD source, who requested anonymity, said.
Jolted by a January surge in unemployment to 4.7 million -- the highest since 1933 -- the two sides had agreed to hold the first such meeting since 1994 to try and agree reforms quickly.

Failure would condemn Waigel's two-year plan to cut 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in taxes to a tough passage through parliament, where the SPD controls the upper house. Wrangling could well drag on into next year's general election campaign and rule out cuts next year to give job-creating investment a boost.

Waigel has also urged the SPD to let through savings measures now backed up in parliament so that Germany can meet the Maastricht treaty's budget deficit ceiling of three percent of GDP this year to qualify for EMU's 1999 start.

Although there was no narrowing of basic differences at the tax summit, coalition sources said Friday's talks would focus on how much to cut corporate taxation. A deal there could open the way to a broader compromise.
The coalition side will be represented at the talks by the parliamentary leader of the Christian Democrats (CDU) Wolfgang Schaeuble, Hermann Otto Solms of the FDP and Waigel.

The SPD will send parliamentary chief Rudolf Scharping, North Rhine-Westphalia finance minister Heinz Schleusser and Hamburg mayor Henning Voscherau. The six may set a second round of full-scale talks next week, government sources said.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl led the coalition team to the talks -- held in the Bonn office of Schleusser's state government next door to the chancellery -- determined to defend plans to slash personal income tax.
The coalition wants the bottom rate to fall to 15 percent from 26 percent and the slash top rate to 39 from 53 percent.

But Schleusser, the SPD's key numbers man, said Waigel's sums did not add up and pinpointed an extra 30 billion marks in revenue shortfalls which would have to be covered either by more borrowing or spending cutbacks.

The coalition is banking on an increase in value-added tax and faster economic growth to make up a financing gap of 44 billion marks. But the SPD opposes a VAT hike, a cut in top income tax and ending tax relief for unsocial work hours.
Schleusser said before the talks began that "the actual financing gap is clearly higher than 44 billion marks and cannot be justified as sound budget policy."
Waigel dismissed the criticism, but said number crunchers from both sides would meet on Tuesday to compare their figures. ($ = 1.676 German Marks)
